The R067 spec is explicit: students 'will not be expected to recall the break-even quantity formula', 'will not be expected to draw a break-even graph but may interpret one or complete a partially completed graph', and 'contribution will not be assessed'. Tone the lesson around interpretation and rearrangement rather than construction. source_lesson.title: Break-Even and Margin of Safety
source_lesson.description: Calculating break-even output, margin of safety and reading break-even diagrams.
source_lesson.content_html:
What Is Break-Even?

Every business needs to know the minimum number of units it must sell to cover all its costs. The break-even point is where total revenue equals total costs — the business is making neither a profit nor a loss. Selling one unit above this point earns profit; one unit below means a loss. Understanding break-even is essential for start-up planning, pricing decisions and securing finance.

Break-even analysis uses three inputs: the selling price per unit, the variable cost per unit, and the total fixed costs. Before we can calculate break-even, we need one intermediate figure: contribution per unit — the selling price minus the variable cost per unit.

Key Fact

Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit
Break-even point (units) = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit
These two formulas must be recalled from memory — they will not be provided in the exam.

Worked Calculation — Break-Even Point

Meadowsweet Preserves sells handmade jams at £6 per jar. Variable costs are £2 per jar. Monthly fixed costs (rent, utilities, insurance) total £2,400.

Step 1 — Contribution per unit: £6 − £2 = £4
Step 2 — Break-even point: £2,400 ÷ £4 = 600 jars per month

This means Meadowsweet must sell 600 jars every month to cover all its costs. If it sells 700 jars, the extra 100 jars each contribute £4 to profit — a total profit of £400. If it sells only 500 jars, the business is £400 in loss (100 jars short × £4 contribution).

Margin of Safety

Once we know the break-even point, we can work out the margin of safety. It tells us how much sales can fall before the business starts making a loss — a useful measure of financial resilience.

Margin of safety = Actual (or budgeted) sales − Break-even sales
In our example, if Meadowsweet actually sells 900 jars per month:
Margin of safety = 900 − 600 = 300 jars
This means sales could drop by 300 jars before any loss would be made. A larger margin of safety means the business is better protected against a fall in demand.

Key Fact

A large margin of safety = the business is well above break-even and can absorb a significant fall in sales. A small margin of safety = the business is close to break-even and vulnerable to any dip in demand or rise in costs.

A break-even diagram plots output on the horizontal axis and costs/revenue (£) on the vertical axis. It contains three lines: total revenue (starts at zero and rises with each unit sold), total costs (starts at the fixed-cost level and rises with variable costs), and fixed costs (a horizontal line).

The point where the total revenue line crosses the total costs line is the break-even point. To the left of this point is the loss zone (costs exceed revenue); to the right is the profit zone (revenue exceeds costs). The vertical gap between total revenue and total costs at any given output is either the profit or the loss at that level.

The margin of safety can be read from the diagram as the horizontal distance between the break-even output and the actual (or budgeted) output level. Students who read diagrams carefully and annotate axes with correct labels pick up easy marks.

Changes to costs or selling price shift the break-even point. Students must be able to interpret these changes both numerically and on a diagram:

If selling price rises: the revenue line becomes steeper — it crosses the total costs line sooner, so break-even output falls. The margin of safety increases (assuming sales stay the same).

If fixed costs rise (e.g. rent increases): the fixed-cost line shifts up, lifting the total costs line parallel to its original position. The revenue line stays the same, so the break-even point moves to the right — more units must be sold to break even. Margin of safety shrinks.

If variable costs rise: the total costs line becomes steeper, pushing break-even point to the right. The contribution per unit falls, so the business needs more sales to cover its fixed costs.

A common exam error is confusing which line moves when costs change. Fixed-cost changes affect the intercept (starting point) of the total-costs line; variable-cost changes affect its gradient (steepness).

Using Break-Even in Decision Making

Break-even analysis is a planning tool, not a guarantee. It assumes that every unit produced is sold, that the selling price stays constant, and that variable costs per unit do not change — assumptions that rarely hold perfectly in a real market. Despite these limitations, it gives entrepreneurs a quick, clear picture of the minimum performance needed to avoid a loss, which is invaluable when writing a business plan or assessing a pricing change.
source_lesson.exam_tip_html: The most common error on break-even calculations is forgetting to calculate contribution per unit as an intermediate step — students sometimes divide fixed costs by the selling price alone, which gives the wrong answer. Always show: Step 1 = Contribution per unit (selling price − variable cost), Step 2 = Break-even (fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit). For “Analyse in Context” questions on break-even, do not just describe the formula — explain what a change in fixed costs or selling price does to the break-even point and margin of safety within the specific scenario. Students who describe changes in isolation without linking them to consequences for the business stall below Secure.
source_lesson.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Break-even point (units) = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit, where contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. These formulas are not given in the exam.
  • Margin of safety = Actual sales − Break-even sales. A larger margin means the business can absorb a bigger fall in demand before making a loss.
  • When fixed costs rise or selling price falls, the break-even point moves to the right (more units needed); when selling price rises or costs fall, it moves to the left (fewer units needed).

practice_questions.text:
A business has fixed costs of £3,600 per month. Each unit sells for £15 and has variable costs of £6.

Use the data to identify the break-even point in units.
practice_questions.marks:
Contribution per unit = £15 − £6 = £9
Break-even = £3,600 ÷ £9 = 400 units [1 mark for correct answer of 400 units]

practice_questions.text:
A business has fixed costs of £4,500 per month. It sells each unit at £25 and variable costs are £10 per unit.

Calculate the break-even point in units.
practice_questions.marks:
Contribution per unit = £25 − £10 = £15
Break-even = £4,500 ÷ £15 = 300 units [2 marks for correct final answer of 300 units; 1 mark if method is correct but arithmetic error is made]

practice_questions.text:
Pinewood Pottery sells ceramic mugs at £18 each. Variable costs are £6 per mug. Monthly fixed costs are £3,600. Pinewood currently sells 400 mugs per month.

Calculate the margin of safety.
practice_questions.marks:
Step 1 — Contribution per unit: £18 − £6 = £12
Step 2 — Break-even: £3,600 ÷ £12 = 300 mugs
Step 3 — Margin of safety: 400 − 300 = 100 mugs
[3 marks: 1 mark for contribution (£12); 1 mark for break-even (300); 1 mark for correct margin of safety (100 mugs). Allow follow-through from earlier errors if method is correct.]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how an increase in fixed costs would affect the break-even point and margin of safety of a small business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks; best two developed points only.

Point 1 — Break-even point rises:
If fixed costs increase, the formula (fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit) produces a higher break-even output. More units must now be sold before the business covers its costs, meaning the profit zone on a break-even diagram shifts to the right.

Point 2 — Margin of safety shrinks:
If actual sales stay the same but break-even output rises, the gap between them narrows. The business is closer to making a loss and is more vulnerable to any fall in demand, seasonal slowdown or competitor price cut.

Point 3 (if offered) — Business response:
To restore the margin of safety, the business could raise its selling price (increasing contribution per unit) or cut variable costs — both would reduce the break-even output, pushing the break-even point back to the left.

1 mark per basic point; +1 for development; +1 for a further analytical step. No context required for Analyse questions at this question type.

practice_questions.text:
Copperkettle Coffee is a small independent café in a market town. It currently sells 900 coffees per month at £3.50 each. Variable costs are £1.00 per coffee. Monthly fixed costs are £1,800.

The owner, Yasmin, is considering raising the price to £4.00 per coffee. She is worried about losing customers.

Analyse how changing the selling price might affect Copperkettle Coffee's break-even point and margin of safety.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Accurate calculation of both break-even and margin of safety at both prices, with a contextualised analysis of the implications. Demonstrates understanding that the higher price reduces the break-even point and increases the margin of safety, but also acknowledges the risk of lost customers (lower actual sales may offset the gain). Judgement is clearly embedded in the café context — e.g. whether an independent café competing on price or quality can absorb a 14% price rise.

Secure (5–7 marks): Calculates or correctly describes the direction of change for at least one scenario. Applies to the Copperkettle context with some development but may not fully explore the risk side (customer loss) or the interaction between price and actual sales volume.

Developing (3–4 marks): Identifies that higher price affects break-even but reasoning is limited. Some attempt to apply the café context but the numbers are not fully used.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Vague reference to break-even or margin of safety with no calculation or meaningful context application.

Calculation guide (for marker reference):
Current: Contribution = £3.50 − £1.00 = £2.50; BEP = £1,800 ÷ £2.50 = 720; MoS = 900 − 720 = 180.
New price: Contribution = £4.00 − £1.00 = £3.00; BEP = £1,800 ÷ £3.00 = 600; MoS (if sales unchanged) = 900 − 600 = 300.

practice_questions.text:
A break-even diagram shows that a business has a break-even point of 500 units and currently sells 650 units.

The business's variable cost per unit then rises from £5 to £7, while the selling price stays at £15 and fixed costs remain at £3,000.

Calculate the new break-even point and identify whether the margin of safety has increased or decreased.
practice_questions.marks:
New contribution = £15 − £7 = £8
New break-even = £3,000 ÷ £8 = 375 units
New margin of safety = 650 − 375 = 275 units (increased from 650 − 500 = 150)
[2 marks: 1 mark for correct new break-even of 375 units; 1 mark for correctly identifying that margin of safety has increased (accept 275 units or 'increased' with supporting calculation)]

knowledge_checks.q: Which formula correctly calculates the break-even point in units?
What does a large margin of safety tell you about a business?
options: Its variable costs are very high
It needs to sell more units to break even
It can absorb a significant fall in sales before making a loss
It is operating at exactly break-even output

knowledge_checks.q: Contribution per unit = Selling price − _____ cost per unit.
The margin of safety = Actual sales − _____ sales.
Match each change to its effect on the break-even point:
right: Break-even point rises (higher starting costs to cover)
Break-even point rises (lower contribution per unit)

glossary_terms.definition: The level of output at which total revenue exactly equals total costs; the business makes neither a profit nor a loss.
The amount left from the selling price of one unit after variable costs have been deducted; it contributes towards covering fixed costs.
The difference between actual (or budgeted) sales and the break-even level of output; the amount by which sales can fall before a loss is made.
Costs that remain constant regardless of the level of output, such as rent and insurance; the starting point on a break-even diagram.
Costs that change in direct proportion to output; a higher variable cost per unit means a lower contribution and a higher break-even point.
The total income a business receives from selling its output, calculated as selling price multiplied by quantity sold.
The area on a break-even diagram to the right of the break-even point, where total revenue exceeds total costs.
The area on a break-even diagram to the left of the break-even point, where total costs exceed total revenue.
